summary: This standards-track document specifies how DNS should treat queries for names ending in home.arpa and designates it as a special-use domain name. It is meant for non-unique use in residential home networks, and it was produced as part of the Homenet work. It gives home devices a place to use local names without clashing with the public DNS.

eli5.summary: Every house can have its own little names, like 'kitchen printer.' This reserves a special name ending so those home names do not mix with real websites.

questions: what domain should i use for home networks
can home.arpa be validated with dnssec
subtitle: A reserved DNS name that home networks can use for local names without colliding with the public internet.

tldr.problem: Home networks need names for things like printers that work without configuration, and the earlier default of '.home' collides with existing uses and leaks to the root name servers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8375 reserves 'home.arpa.' as a special-use domain name of local significance, tells resolvers not to forward its queries, and delegates it insecurely under '.arpa.' to black hole servers.
tldr.outcome: It replaces '.home' as the default domain in the Home Networking Control Protocol, updating RFC 7788. Names under it are not globally unique and cannot be validated with DNSSEC unless a trust anchor is configured by hand.

facts.label: Delegation
facts.value: Insecure, no DS record, black hole servers

facts.label: Forwarding
facts.value: Queries must not leave the homenet

today: RFC 8375 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 7788 so that HNCP uses home.arpa. instead of .home.

sections.title: Why home.arpa Exists
sections.content:
Devices in a home network (a homenet) need names that are unique inside that network, and the naming has to work without user configuration and even if the ISP delegates no name. RFC 8375 reserves home.arpa. as the default name for this purpose, with scope limited to each individual homenet.

It corrects an error in RFC 7788, the Home Networking Control Protocol (HNCP), which used .home. That name was chosen as the most user-friendly, but existing uses of .home may conflict, and evidence shows .home queries often leak out and reach the root name servers. There is also no process to request a delegation in the root for the IETF, which does not administer that zone, whereas there is an existing process for names under .arpa.. So all unregistered uses of .home are deprecated.

Use is not restricted to HNCP networks. The name is meant for local name service in residential homenets generally.
sections.eli5: The old special name, '.home', could clash with real names out on the internet. A new name under 'arpa' is safe because the internet's librarians can reserve it properly.

sections.title: General Guidance
sections.content:
Names ending in .home.arpa. refer to a zone served locally. Its contents are unique only to a particular homenet and are not globally unique. Such names point to nodes and services in the home, for example a printer or a toaster. Identical queries can therefore give different answers on different homenets.

Queries for these names are resolved by local resolvers and MUST NOT be recursively forwarded to servers outside the logical boundaries of the homenet.

The authors admit the name is an imperfect way to signal to readers that a name refers to a device in the home, since users may sometimes need to see, remember and type it.
sections.eli5: A name like 'printer.home.arpa' only means something inside your own house. Asking the outside world about it would be like asking a stranger where your kitchen is.

sections.title: How Resolvers and Software Must Behave
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the considerations of RFC 6761 for special-use names.

  • Applications SHOULD NOT treat these names differently from others, and there is no basis for trusting them.
  • Name resolution APIs and libraries MUST NOT treat them as special, except that they may need to avoid bypassing the locally configured recursive resolvers. A host using some other configured resolver may fail to resolve them, so hosts are permitted to use the locally provided resolvers for home.arpa. anyway.
  • Recursive resolvers MUST transparently support DNSSEC queries (DNSSEC records and queries with the DO bit set), and validation is strongly encouraged. Unless configured otherwise they MUST follow RFC 6303, so queries for home.arpa. and its subdomains MUST NOT be forwarded. The one exception is a query for a DS record with the DO bit set, which MUST return a correct answer including proof of nonexistence.
  • Resolvers usable in a homenet MUST be configurable to forward home.arpa. queries to an authoritative server for it. A resolver may also answer them authoritatively itself.
  • Authoritative servers need no special processing, but one that checks for a delegation before answering MUST be configurable to skip or ignore that check for home.arpa..
sections.eli5: Your home's helper keeps questions about home names inside the house. The only thing it checks with the outside is whether the name has an official lock on it, and the answer is no.

sections.title: The Update to HNCP
sections.content:
RFC 8375 updates the last paragraph of Section 8 of RFC 7788. Where it said .home is the default network-wide zone, it now says home.arpa. is the default. An administrator MAY still announce a Domain-Name TLV to use a different domain, and when several are announced the node with the greatest node identifier wins.

The new text adds that home.arpa. needs no special resolution protocol. Names whose rightmost two labels are home.arpa. are resolved with the DNS protocol of RFC 1035.
sections.eli5: The rule book for home networks used to say 'use .home'. It now says 'use home.arpa', and the rest of the rules stay the same.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Answers for home.arpa. names are expected to come from a server of the current homenet, but they MUST NOT be considered more trustworthy than any other DNS answer. Because the zone is not globally scoped and cannot be secured with DNSSEC from the root trust anchor, a standard query cannot reveal which homenet an answer belongs to, so roaming users may see surprising results. A mechanism to tell homenets apart securely is out of scope and left to future work.

The advice in RFC 6303 to install local trust anchors is not practicable, because homenets have no way to configure them on hosts, and a host with one trust anchor could not use other homes' instances.

The delegation has to be insecure. A DS record cannot be placed in .arpa because no one key would work for a non-unique zone, and relying on authenticated denial of existence would require every validating resolver to treat home.arpa. specially. So DNSSEC signing and validation inside the zone is not possible unless a trust anchor is configured manually.

The exception letting hosts use local resolvers despite manual configuration has security and privacy implications. The authors lack operational experience to decide and encourage implementors to weigh their deployment context.
sections.eli5: Because every house has its own 'kitchen', nobody can issue one official proof that a particular 'kitchen' is the right one. So treat home names as helpful hints, not as proven facts.

sections.title: Delegation and IANA Actions
sections.content:
For the name to be fully functional, home.arpa. must be delegated in the .arpa. zone. The delegation MUST NOT include a DS record and MUST point to one or more black hole servers, for example blackhole-1.iana.org. and blackhole-2.iana.org.. Leaving it unsigned breaks the DNSSEC chain of trust, which stops a validating stub resolver from rejecting names published under home.arpa. on a homenet name server. The arpa domain is operated by IANA under the authority of the Internet Architecture Board, with no other registrars.

IANA has recorded home.arpa. in the Special-Use Domain Names registry and implemented the delegation with IAB approval. It also created the subregistry "Transport-Independent Locally-Served DNS Zone Registry" and added home.arpa. there with the description "Homenet Special-Use Domain". Registration follows "IETF Review".
sections.eli5: The internet's librarians wrote 'home.arpa' in their book of reserved names and pointed it at a dead end on purpose, so it never gets a global answer.
